videos.title: Justin's Perspective on Blindness
videos.description: Justin Salas, our Accessibility Champion at Perspective Tester, guides us through his world of web navigation.

alternative.text: Justin sits facing the camera in a dark T-shirt against a plain wall, hands clasped, a tattoo sleeve on his left forearm.

alternative.speaker: Justin Salas
alternative.text: My name is Justin. I work for Perspective Tester, and I'm blind or low vision, and I'm a native assistive technology user. My vision presents with no central vision and limited peripheral vision. Without assistive technology, I certainly don't think I would be where I am today.

Over Justin's shoulder: a large monitor shows the Google home page, and he gestures at it from his chair. Then the screen magnifies until the “G” of the Google logo and the mouse pointer fill the display.

alternative.speaker: Justin Salas
alternative.text: You know, I can't see the screen when it's back this far. I see a little bit of light and contrast in certain places, but I really need to get down on the individual letter size to see what things are. I use screen readers and zoom and all the different tools to help me navigate life and to be as independent as I possibly can. And so when it doesn't work, it's extremely frustrating. It's pretty limiting, but I can still function and get around.
Justin leans in close to the monitor. At this magnification only part of the Google logo fits on screen; he moves the pointer to the search box and types.

alternative.speaker: Justin Salas
alternative.text: With nothing in the middle, I can't see my screens very well. I use assistive technology in a myriad of different ways. When I'm using my computer, I'm zooming down to individual letters and navigating my screens that way.

Justin pans across a magnified website a few letters at a time, the text blurring as it moves: “Sign in”, a yellow “Join now” button and a black banner with “Get tickets” in yellow. Zoomed out, the page shows a notification popup with “Later” and “Subscribe” buttons.

alternative.speaker: Justin Salas
alternative.text: Sometimes it's really difficult to read long paragraphs of text with one letter on the screen at a time, and so I use VoiceOver at a pretty fast speaking rate. It's really important that a lot of websites and mobile apps work well with screen readers, to have it read it to me.
At normal size, Justin scrolls through the website's menu and articles. Then he zooms in on a blue heading beginning “Our F”, with the text cursor over it.

alternative.speaker: Justin Salas
alternative.text: It's really amazing, but when it doesn't work, it creates huge limiting factors.

alternative.speaker: Justin Salas
alternative.text: My name's Justin, and this is my perspective.

videos.title: What Makes the Web Inaccessible?
videos.description: Justin Salas shares one key reason digital experiences become inaccessible.

alternative.text: Over Justin's shoulder as he sits at a large monitor showing a website. On-screen title: “What makes a website inaccessible?”

alternative.speaker: Justin Salas
alternative.text: So we're going to talk about things that are not accessible. It's not necessarily just a lack of trying. A lot of the times, people just don't know. So, no disrespect, but, like, this kind of thing is frustrating.
Justin magnifies the site's menu until the word “NEWS” fills the screen in dark text on white.

alternative.speaker: Justin Salas
alternative.text: Like, this level of contrast is fantastic. This black on white background, it's easy to see. But usually then I try and get it into the frame, and all of a sudden it goes yellow.
When the pointer hovers over “NEWS”, the link turns pale yellow on white.

alternative.speaker: Justin Salas
alternative.text: But now the contrast ratio is bad enough that I can't hardly tell what I'm looking at. That's a big, big sticking point.

A notification popup has appeared: a dark square logo with the letter “C”, the text “Subscribe to our notifications and updates. You can disable anytime.”, a “Later” link and a blue “Subscribe” button. Magnified, Justin sees only fragments of it at a time.

alternative.speaker: Justin Salas
alternative.text: None of this is clickable at the moment, 'cause this popup has occurred. So it can be difficult. It's a popup showing up on a web page, and you can't get out of it, or you can't find it. This is pretty confusing. The popup is only findable based on this contrast here, between this and this. But otherwise it's difficult to see it's even there.
Justin moves the pointer onto “Later”, then zooms out to the whole page and back in. Hovering over the “PEOPLE” link turns it yellow.

alternative.speaker: Justin Salas
alternative.text: So sometimes I'll be clicking around on a site and I'm like, why is nothing working? And then I'm looking around the page, I'm trying to figure out what's what, and I finally find that, oh, there's a popup. I need to close that. And then things start functioning again.
End card: the Perspective Tester logo.

paragraph_4: Watch how Perspective Tester brings engineering equity to digital experiences with practical, human-centered accessibility work.
